screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why authentication and authorization are the foundation of a secure MongoDB deployment. Authentication checks that a connection is who it claims to be, and authorization decides what that verified identity can actually do. We will focus on SCRAM, the default and recommended authentication mechanism, and then move into how to create an administrative user, enable authentication safely, and design Role-Based Access Control policies that follow the principle of least privilege. You will see concrete examples for creating built-in and custom roles, plus a hands-on activity that walks through starting mongod without authentication, creating an admin user, restarting with authentication enabled, and testing a restricted user’s permissions. Think about one service in your application that only needs to read data — how would you restrict its access so a compromise can’t expose everything?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › User Authentication and Authorization
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

User Authentication and Authorization

Secure MongoDB by verifying user identities and granting only the permissions required for each role. This reduces risk and helps meet compliance needs.

In this lesson
SCRAM, RBAC, admin setup, custom roles, testing.
Coming up
Hands-on role creation and verification steps.
Why it matters
Prevents unauthorized reads, writes, and admin changes.
Orientation
You’ll practice creating an admin user, enabling authentication, and then designing custom roles so application users have exactly the privileges they need.
Concept Map
A
Authentication (SCRAM)
Proves identity using salted password hashes.
B
Authorization (RBAC)
Assign roles to grant specific privileges.
C
Principle of Least Privilege
Grant only required actions on resources.
Explore Key Topics
SCRAM: default, salted hashes, resists clear-text leaks.
RBAC: built-in roles, custom roles, and scope per database.
Admin setup: create admin before enabling auth to avoid lockout.

screens.title: Authentication vs Authorization
screens.narratorSegment: Authentication and authorization are related but distinct security concepts. Authentication answers the question, "Who are you?" It confirms identity using credentials such as a username and password. In MongoDB, the server verifies credentials with a stored salted hash rather than the clear-text password. Authorization answers, "What are you allowed to do?" Once a user is authenticated, RBAC determines actions like find, insert, update, or administrative commands on specific resources. A simple analogy is entering a building: authentication is the guard checking your ID at reception; authorization is the badge that controls which rooms you can access. A concrete example: an application service may authenticate as inventoryAppUser, but authorization restricts it to read products and write audits only. A common misconception is assuming authentication alone is sufficient. Without authorization, any authenticated user could perform unrestricted actions. Conversely, authorization without authentication is meaningless because the system cannot associate privileges to an identity. Key takeaway: implement both controls together and test both allowed and denied paths so you verify that identity and permissions are enforced as intended. Which account in your stack should have the narrowest privileges?

keyIdea.title: Distinction
keyIdea.text: Authentication proves identity; authorization assigns permissions to that identity. Both are required for secure access control.

content.html:
Core Concept › Chapter 8.1 › Authentication vs Authorization
Definition

Authentication

Verifies who a client is using credentials. MongoDB stores salted password hashes and validates via SCRAM.

Analogy

Think of a security guard checking an ID. That check proves identity but does not say which rooms you may enter.

Common misconception
Believing authentication alone prevents misuse. You must pair it with authorization to restrict actions.
Definition

Authorization

Determines what an authenticated user may do, using roles that grant specific privileges on databases and collections.

  • Privileges are actions such as find, insert, update, and remove.
  • Roles group privileges and can be assigned to many users.
  • Scope matters: roles can be database-specific or cluster-wide.
Key Takeaway

Treat authentication as identity proof and authorization as permission control. Both layers together enforce secure access.

screens.title: SCRAM: MongoDB's primary authentication mechanism
screens.narratorSegment: SCRAM stands for Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism. In MongoDB, SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256 are supported; SCRAM prevents clear-text password transmission by using a challenge-response protocol and stores a salted hash of the password on the server. The salt makes precomputed attacks and rainbow tables ineffective because each stored hash depends on a unique salt. In practice, when a client authenticates, the server issues a challenge and the client proves knowledge of the password without sending it verbatim. A concrete example: when you create a user with a password, MongoDB stores the salted hash; if an attacker copies the internal user data, they won’t have plain passwords. A common misconception is that storing hashes alone is sufficient; the use of a salt and modern hashing algorithm increases cost for attackers. For enterprise environments, MongoDB can integrate external systems like Kerberos, LDAP, or x.509 certificates. For most application deployments, SCRAM provides a secure, simple default. Key takeaway: prefer SCRAM for application users and avoid transmitting or storing plain-text credentials in code or config files. SCRAM: MongoDB's primary authentication mechanism means scram avoids clear-text passwords and stores salted hashes so authentication data remains resilient against common attacks.. In practical terms, why scram is recommended and how salted hashes protect credentials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Chapter 8.1 › SCRAM

SCRAM Basics

SCRAM is a challenge-response protocol that protects credentials and uses salted password hashes on the server.

What it prevents
No clear-text passwords over the wire. Salted hashes resist precomputed attacks.
Common choices
SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256. Use the strongest supported algorithm for your environment.
Concrete Example
When you run db.createUser with a password, MongoDB stores a salted hash. On authentication, the client proves knowledge without sending the password itself.
Key Takeaway

SCRAM is the secure default for application users because it avoids clear-text passwords and uses salts to harden stored credentials.

screens.title: Safe admin creation and enabling authentication
screens.narratorSegment: A critical operational step is creating an administrative user before enabling authentication. If you enable authentication on a running mongod instance without any admin user, you can lock yourself out. The safe process starts with stopping mongod if it is running with auth enabled incorrectly. Start mongod without authentication so you can connect freely. Connect to the admin database, and run db. createUser to create an admin user with the userAdminAnyDatabase role. Once the admin exists, stop mongod and restart it with the --auth flag so the server requires credentials on new connections. Example commands in the hands-on section show mongo shell usage and connection flags. A common mistake is assuming the credentials will work without specifying the correct authenticationDatabase during connection; the authentication database is where the user was created, commonly admin for administrative accounts. After restarting with auth, authenticate as the admin user to perform further user and role management. Key takeaway: always create the admin account first, then enable --auth, and confirm authentication works with the proper authenticationDatabase parameter. Safe admin creation and enabling authentication means create admin while auth is off, then restart with --auth. verify connections use the correct authenticationdatabase.. In practical terms, the correct sequence to avoid locking yourself out. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Process Flow › Chapter 8.1 › Admin creation & auth
Follow these numbered steps to avoid lockout.
1
Start mongod without authentication
This allows initial user creation without credential checks.
2
Create the admin user
Use the admin database and assign userAdminAnyDatabase role to manage users.
3
Restart mongod with --auth
The server will now require authentication for connections.
4
Connect and authenticate as admin
Specify the correct authenticationDatabase (often admin) when connecting.
Example command
mongo --port 27017
use admin
 db.createUser({ user: 'superAdmin', pwd: 'superSecurePassword', roles: [{ role: 'userAdminAnyDatabase', db: 'admin' }] })

screens.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
screens.narratorSegment: RBAC organizes privileges into roles and assigns roles to users. A privilege specifies an action, such as find or insert, on a resource like database. collection. A role is a named collection of privileges and can inherit other roles. MongoDB ships with many built-in roles—read, readWrite, dbAdmin, clusterMonitor and more—that cover common operational duties. You can also create custom roles to precisely express your application requirements. For example, a custom role might grant find on products and insert on audits within the inventory database. Roles have scope: a role granted on a specific database confines privileges to that database, while cluster-level roles grant broader capabilities. A frequent pitfall is over-privileging users by assigning broad roles like readAnyDatabase or userAdminAnyDatabase without necessity. The principle of least privilege recommends granting only what is needed. A practical pattern is to create an application-specific role, test it by connecting as the application user, and then iterate until the smallest set of privileges remains. Key takeaway: design roles to match real operational boundaries and review them regularly to reduce your attack surface. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) means roles group privileges on resources; scope roles narrowly to implement least privilege and simplify management.. In practical terms, how roles, privileges, and resources combine to enforce permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture › Chapter 8.1 › RBAC

Roles, Privileges, Resources

Role
Named set of privileges; can inherit other roles.
Privilege
An action such as find, insert, update, remove on a resource.
Resource
A specific database or collection to which a privilege applies.
Built-in roles
Examples include read, readWrite, dbAdmin, userAdmin, clusterMonitor, and backup. Use built-ins when they match needs to avoid reinventing roles.
Custom role example
appInventoryRole with find on inventory.products and insert/update/remove on inventory.audits.
Scope caution
Roles scoped to admin or cluster-wide give broad power—review them carefully.
Key Takeaway

Design roles to reflect real duties, grant minimum privileges, and prefer custom roles for narrowly scoped application access.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Chapter 8.1 › User & Role Creation

Example commands

Use these exact mongo shell calls to create an admin, define a custom role, and add an application user.
// Create admin in the admin database
use admin
 db.createUser({ user: "adminUser", pwd: "securePassword123", roles: [{ role: "userAdminAnyDatabase", db: "admin" }] })

// Switch to inventory and create a custom role
use inventory
 db.createRole({
   role: "appInventoryRole",
   privileges: [
     { resource: { db: "inventory", collection: "products" }, actions: [ "find" ] },
     { resource: { db: "inventory", collection: "audits" }, actions: [ "insert", "update", "remove" ] }
   ],
   roles: []
 })

// Create application user and assign the role
 db.createUser({ user: "inventoryAppUser", pwd: "anotherSecurePassword456", roles: [ { role: "appInventoryRole", db: "inventory" } ] })

// Verify
 db.getUser("inventoryAppUser")
Concrete example
inventoryAppUser can find products and insert/update/remove audits only.
Common mistake
Enabling auth before creating admin or connecting with wrong authenticationDatabase leads to AuthenticationFailed errors.

screens.title: Built-in roles vs Custom roles
screens.narratorSegment: MongoDB provides many built-in roles to cover common operational tasks. Use built-in roles like read, readWrite, dbAdmin, and clusterMonitor when they closely match the responsibilities you want to assign. Built-ins reduce complexity and testing overhead. However, if your application needs very specific access — for example, read access to one collection and write access to another — a custom role is preferable. Custom roles let you enumerate precise privileges and keep permissions narrowly scoped. The provided inventory example demonstrates a custom role granting find on products and insert/update/remove on audits. A practical approach is to prefer built-ins for standard administrative accounts, and custom roles for application users where least privilege matters. A common misconception is to assume built-ins are always safer. In fact, some built-ins (readAnyDatabase, userAdminAnyDatabase) are broad and risk over-privilege. Key takeaway: choose the simplest built-in role that meets needs; when it doesn’t, create a custom role and test it thoroughly with a dedicated user account. Built-in roles vs Custom roles means prefer built-in roles where appropriate; create custom roles when you need precise, collection-level permissions.. In practical terms, when to use built-in roles and when to craft custom ones. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Chapter 8.1 › Built-in vs Custom
Built-in Roles
  • Predefined for common tasks like read, readWrite, dbAdmin.
  • Quick to assign and well-tested for standard use cases.
  • Avoid broad ones unless necessary (readAnyDatabase, userAdminAnyDatabase).
Custom Roles
  • Define explicit privileges on resources, down to collection-level actions.
  • Ideal for application users requiring narrow permissions.
  • Requires testing to ensure no privilege gaps or accidental excess.
Practical rule

Start with the least-privileged built-in role that fits. If it’s too broad, design a custom role tailored to your app’s exact needs and verify via tests.

screens.title: Testing user permissions

Test sequence

1. Connect as restricted user
Include authenticationDatabase matching the user’s creation DB.
2. Execute allowed action
Expect success for operations the role permits, e.g., find on allowed collections.

Example test from chapter
Connect as taskUser and run db.tasks.find (should succeed), then try db.tasks.insertOne (should fail), then db.logs.insertOne (should succeed) when the role grants logs insert.

screens.title: Scope of roles: database vs cluster
screens.narratorSegment: Roles in MongoDB have scope and that scope determines where privileges apply. A role defined and granted on a particular database typically grants permissions only within that database. For example, a role granted on the inventory database allows access to collections inside inventory, but not to other databases unless explicitly allowed. In contrast, cluster-level or admin database roles like userAdminAnyDatabase or clusterMonitor can affect the entire deployment. Built-in cluster roles are necessary for some administrative tasks, but they should be used sparingly because they broaden the attack surface. When designing your RBAC strategy, decide which roles require cluster-level scope and which can be limited to a single database. A practical pattern is to keep application roles database-scoped and reserve admin or cluster roles for platform operators. A common misconception is that assigning an admin role to a user is harmless; in reality, broad roles can permit user creation across all databases and should be given only to trusted operators. Key takeaway: scope roles narrowly and audit assignments regularly. Scope of roles: database vs cluster means grant roles at the narrowest scope necessary — prefer database-scoped roles for applications and reserve cluster roles for operators.. In practical terms, understanding where a role applies and its impact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Hands-on Activity › Chapter 8.1 › Lab: taskManagerRole

Terminal demo steps

  1. Start mongod without auth: mongod --port 27017 --dbpath /data/db
  2. Create admin in admin database if needed using db.createUser.
  3. Restart mongod with --auth to enable authentication.
  4. Connect as admin and create project_management and insert sample tasks.
  5. Create taskManagerRole granting find on tasks and insert/update/remove on logs.
  6. Create taskUser and assign taskManagerRole, then test as that user.
Quick command snippet
use project_management
 db.tasks.insertOne({ title: "Design UI", status: "pending", assignee: "Alice" })
 db.createRole({ role: "taskManagerRole", privileges: [ { resource: { db: "project_management", collection: "tasks" }, actions: [ "find" ] }, { resource: { db: "project_management", collection: "logs" }, actions: [ "insert", "update", "remove" ] } ], roles: [] })
 db.createUser({ user: "taskUser", pwd: "taskUserPassword", roles: [ { role: "taskManagerRole", db: "project_management" } ] })
Key Takeaway

Run the full create → assign → test cycle so you catch scope and authenticationDatabase issues early.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Several practical pitfalls appear frequently when teams configure MongoDB security. The first is enabling authentication before creating an administrative user — this causes accidental lockout and often requires manual recovery. Avoid it by creating admin while auth is off and then restarting with --auth. The second is authenticating against the wrong database. Users are scoped to the database where they were created; if you connect with the wrong authenticationDatabase parameter, authentication fails even with correct credentials. The third is over-privileging: assigning overly broad roles like readAnyDatabase increases exposure. Apply the principle of least privilege and prefer custom, narrowly scoped roles for application services. The fourth pitfall is storing credentials in code or plain config files; instead, use environment variables or a secrets manager in production and rotate passwords regularly. Finally, assume that copying internal user data without salts is not equivalent to having passwords; salts and SCRAM reduce the effectiveness of stolen credential artifacts. Key takeaway: follow the safe setup sequence, scope roles narrowly, test connections with the correct auth DB, and protect credentials off-disk for production systems. Common mistakes and how to avoid them means avoid enabling auth too early, using wrong auth db, over-privileging roles, and hardcoding credentials; test and rotate secrets regularly.. Warning › Chapter 8.1 › Common Pitfalls

Avoid these mistakes

Enabling auth before admin
Create admin first, then restart with --auth to avoid lockout.
Wrong authenticationDatabase
Authenticate against the database where the user was created, or you will get AuthenticationFailed errors.
Over-privileging
Grant minimal permissions and prefer custom roles instead of broad built-ins where possible.
Hardcoded credentials
Use a secrets manager and rotate passwords; never store production credentials in source code.
Remediation checklist
  • Create admin before enabling auth.
  • Use correct authenticationDatabase in connections.
  • Design roles with least privilege and test them.
  • Secure credentials and rotate regularly.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize three essential ideas to remember. First, authentication verifies identity and should use SCRAM so passwords are never sent in clear text; MongoDB stores salted password hashes to make stolen user data far less useful to attackers. Second, authorization uses RBAC: group privileges into roles and assign them to users. Design roles that match real responsibilities and prefer narrow, database-scoped roles for application users. Third, always follow the safe operational sequence: create an admin user before enabling authentication, connect with the correct authenticationDatabase, and test both allowed and denied operations for any new user. These practices together reduce the risk of unauthorized access, prevent accidental lockouts, and make your system easier to audit. As you work through the hands-on activity, keep these concepts in mind so you can build secure and maintainable access controls.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why authentication and authorization are the foundation of a secure MongoDB deployment. Authentication checks that a connection is who it claims to be, and authorization decides what that verified identity can actually do. We will focus on SCRAM, the default and recommended authentication mechanism, and then move into how to create an administrative user, enable authentication safely, and design Role-Based Access Control policies that follow the principle of least privilege. You will see concrete examples for creating built-in and custom roles, plus a hands-on activity that walks through starting mongod without authentication, creating an admin user, restarting with authentication enabled, and testing a restricted user’s permissions. Along the way I’ll highlight common mistakes, such as enabling auth before creating an admin user or using overly broad roles. By the end of this chapter you will be able to create users and roles, scope privileges to specific databases and collections, and test access using the authenticationDatabase parameter. Think about one service in your application that only needs to read data — how would you restrict its access so a compromise can’t expose everything?

Over the next screens you will learn four concrete skills. First, you will understand authentication and authorization — what they are and why both are required for database security. I will give you a definition, an everyday analogy, and a short example so this distinction is clear. Second, you will learn to create and manage users and an administrative account, including the safe sequence for enabling authentication so you do not lock yourself out. Third, you will differentiate and configure authentication mechanisms, with emphasis on SCRAM as the default and how it stores salted password hashes rather than clear text. Fourth, you will design and apply Role-Based Access Control. That includes using built-in roles, composing custom roles for fine-grained access, and applying the principle of least privilege. Each objective is paired with a competency milestone so you can test your setup. By the end you’ll be able to demonstrate a restricted user who can perform allowed actions and is prevented from unauthorized operations.

This second objectives screen lays out the practical checks you will perform. You will start mongod without authentication, create an admin user, then restart with the auth flag so the server enforces credentials. Practice connecting with the correct authenticationDatabase — this detail commonly causes authentication failures. You will also create a custom role scoped to a specific database and collections, assign it to a new user, and then test both allowed and disallowed operations from that user account. Finally, review the user and role listings to confirm permissions. Each check is deliberate: starting mongod without auth temporarily allows setup, authenticating the admin prevents lockout, and testing verifies the system behaves as expected. The hands-on activity in the chapter mirrors these steps. Successful completion demonstrates you can both configure authentication safely and apply RBAC to protect application data while avoiding over-privilege.

Authentication and authorization are related but distinct security concepts. Authentication answers the question, "Who are you?" It confirms identity using credentials such as a username and password. In MongoDB, the server verifies credentials with a stored salted hash rather than the clear-text password. Authorization answers, "What are you allowed to do?" Once a user is authenticated, RBAC determines actions like find, insert, update, or administrative commands on specific resources. A simple analogy is entering a building: authentication is the guard checking your ID at reception; authorization is the badge that controls which rooms you can access. A concrete example: an application service may authenticate as inventoryAppUser, but authorization restricts it to read products and write audits only. A common misconception is assuming authentication alone is sufficient. Without authorization, any authenticated user could perform unrestricted actions. Conversely, authorization without authentication is meaningless because the system cannot associate privileges to an identity. Key takeaway: implement both controls together and test both allowed and denied paths so you verify that identity and permissions are enforced as intended. Which account in your stack should have the narrowest privileges?

SCRAM stands for Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism. In MongoDB, SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256 are supported; SCRAM prevents clear-text password transmission by using a challenge-response protocol and stores a salted hash of the password on the server. The salt makes precomputed attacks and rainbow tables ineffective because each stored hash depends on a unique salt. In practice, when a client authenticates, the server issues a challenge and the client proves knowledge of the password without sending it verbatim. A concrete example: when you create a user with a password, MongoDB stores the salted hash; if an attacker copies the internal user data, they won’t have plain passwords. A common misconception is that storing hashes alone is sufficient; the use of a salt and modern hashing algorithm increases cost for attackers. For enterprise environments, MongoDB can integrate external systems like Kerberos, LDAP, or x.509 certificates. For most application deployments, SCRAM provides a secure, simple default. Key takeaway: prefer SCRAM for application users and avoid transmitting or storing plain-text credentials in code or config files. SCRAM: MongoDB's primary authentication mechanism means scram avoids clear-text passwords and stores salted hashes so authentication data remains resilient against common attacks.. In practical terms, why scram is recommended and how salted hashes protect credentials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A critical operational step is creating an administrative user before enabling authentication. If you enable authentication on a running mongod instance without any admin user, you can lock yourself out. The safe process starts with stopping mongod if it is running with auth enabled incorrectly. Start mongod without authentication so you can connect freely. Connect to the admin database, and run db. createUser to create an admin user with the userAdminAnyDatabase role. Once the admin exists, stop mongod and restart it with the --auth flag so the server requires credentials on new connections. Example commands in the hands-on section show mongo shell usage and connection flags. A common mistake is assuming the credentials will work without specifying the correct authenticationDatabase during connection; the authentication database is where the user was created, commonly admin for administrative accounts. After restarting with auth, authenticate as the admin user to perform further user and role management. Key takeaway: always create the admin account first, then enable --auth, and confirm authentication works with the proper authenticationDatabase parameter. RBAC organizes privileges into roles and assigns roles to users. A privilege specifies an action, such as find or insert, on a resource like database. collection. A role is a named collection of privileges and can inherit other roles. MongoDB ships with many built-in roles—read, readWrite, dbAdmin, clusterMonitor and more—that cover common operational duties. You can also create custom roles to precisely express your application requirements. For example, a custom role might grant find on products and insert on audits within the inventory database. Roles have scope: a role granted on a specific database confines privileges to that database, while cluster-level roles grant broader capabilities. A frequent pitfall is over-privileging users by assigning broad roles like readAnyDatabase or userAdminAnyDatabase without necessity. The principle of least privilege recommends granting only what is needed. A practical pattern is to create an application-specific role, test it by connecting as the application user, and then iterate until the smallest set of privileges remains. Key takeaway: design roles to match real operational boundaries and review them regularly to reduce your attack surface. Several practical pitfalls appear frequently when teams configure MongoDB security. The first is enabling authentication before creating an administrative user — this causes accidental lockout and often requires manual recovery. Avoid it by creating admin while auth is off and then restarting with --auth. The second is authenticating against the wrong database. Users are scoped to the database where they were created; if you connect with the wrong authenticationDatabase parameter, authentication fails even with correct credentials. The third is over-privileging: assigning overly broad roles like readAnyDatabase increases exposure. Apply the principle of least privilege and prefer custom, narrowly scoped roles for application services. The fourth pitfall is storing credentials in code or plain config files; instead, use environment variables or a secrets manager in production and rotate passwords regularly. Finally, assume that copying internal user data without salts is not equivalent to having passwords; salts and SCRAM reduce the effectiveness of stolen credential artifacts. Key takeaway: follow the safe setup sequence, scope roles narrowly, test connections with the correct auth DB, and protect credentials off-disk for production systems. Let's summarize three essential ideas to remember. First, authentication verifies identity and should use SCRAM so passwords are never sent in clear text; MongoDB stores salted password hashes to make stolen user data far less useful to attackers. Second, authorization uses RBAC: group privileges into roles and assign them to users. Design roles that match real responsibilities and prefer narrow, database-scoped roles for application users. Third, always follow the safe operational sequence: create an admin user before enabling authentication, connect with the correct authenticationDatabase, and test both allowed and denied operations for any new user. These practices together reduce the risk of unauthorized access, prevent accidental lockouts, and make your system easier to audit.
